content: Winging of the scapula occurs due to weakness in the thoracoscapular muscles, which are responsible for stabilizing the scapula against the chest wall during shoulder movements. In facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD), and occasionally in other forms of muscular dystrophy, there is a selective weakening of these thoracoscapular muscles. Interestingly, other shoulder muscles, such as the deltoid, may remain unaffected. This imbalance between muscle groups leads to pronounced scapular winging and a significant reduction in shoulder function. Historically, various surgical and non-surgical approaches have been employed to stabilize the scapula in individuals with muscular dystrophy. This review specifically evaluates the available evidence regarding the effectiveness of these scapular fixation techniques, with a particular focus on their use in facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy. The primary objective of this review was to assess the relative efficacy of scapular fixation methods in improving upper limb function in individuals with muscular dystrophy, especially those with FSHD. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Trials Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Medline, and EMBASE, covering studies published up to July 2009. Additionally, experts in the field and authors of relevant trials were contacted to identify any further studies. The inclusion criteria for this review encompassed all reports of scapular fixation in muscular dystrophy, including both quasi-randomized and randomized controlled trials. These studies needed to compare any form of scapular fixation, whether surgical or non-surgical, in individuals of all ages and disease severities who exhibited scapular winging due to muscular dystrophy. The primary outcome measure was an objective improvement in shoulder abduction. Secondary outcomes included patient-reported improvements in performing daily activities, cosmetic outcomes, subjective pain relief, and the proportion of patients experiencing significant postoperative complications. Upon reviewing the available literature, no randomized controlled trials were identified. Consequently, the review is based on non-randomized studies and observational data. The findings suggest that while operative interventions may provide benefits, as indicated by observational studies, these potential advantages must be weighed against the risks of postoperative immobilization, the need for extensive physiotherapy, and the possibility of complications. The authors conclude that there is no robust evidence from randomized trials to definitively support the efficacy of surgical interventions for scapular fixation in muscular dystrophy. They acknowledge the challenges of conducting randomized trials in this context but recommend the establishment of a case registry and the adoption of a standardized assessment protocol. Such measures would facilitate more accurate comparisons of the various techniques and improve the quality of evidence in this field.
